It was popular around 1850, and at the end of the nineteenth century players bent the box boards to adjust the vibration. After abolition it passed to the criollo population, and in the twentieth century, under the influence of the Afro-Peruvian music group founded in 1969, its standing in Peruvian black music rose and it became its emblem. In 1977 Caitro Soto and Paco de Lucía brought it to Spain; researchers hold that Pepe Ébano introduced it to flamenco. In 2001 Peru's national cultural body listed it as national cultural heritage, and in 2014 the Organization of American States declared it "the instrument Peru gave to the Americas".

The cajón is a box-shaped wooden percussion instrument from Peru, a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 111.221. It is a six-sided wooden box with one face of thinner plywood as the striking face and a round hole in the back for the sound to come out. The player usually sits on the box with the feet on either side and strikes the face and sides with the palms, fingers, brushes or drumsticks. It is used mainly in the criollo music of Afro-Peruvian music, and has also entered flamenco and Latin American music, and is often heard in street performance and small accompanying line-ups.
